prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

PARIS, France (CNN) -- Hundreds of French workers, angry about proposed layoffs at a Caterpillar factory, were holding executives of the company hostage Tuesday, a spokesman for the workers said. Caterpillar's French staff say they are angry about a lack of negotiations over layoffs. It is at least the third time this month that French workers threatened with cutbacks have blockaded managers in their offices to demand negotiations. Executives were released unharmed in both previous situations. The latest incident started Tuesday morning at the office of the construction equipment company in the southeastern city of Grenoble. The workers were angry that Caterpillar had proposed cutting more than 700 jobs and would not negotiate, said Nicolas Benoit, a spokesman for the workers' union. They did not want to harm the Caterpillar executives, Benoit told CNN. One hostage was released Tuesday evening leaving workers with four captives inside the Caterpillar building. The released man was a human resources director identified only as Mr. Petit, because he has heart problems, union representative Bernard Patrick told CNN. Petit had a heart attack a few weeks ago, Patrick said. The four others still being held are Nicolas Polutnik, the head of operations; two other executives; and Petit's personal assistant, he said. About 500 employees were also outside the building protesting. A top Caterpillar executive called the hostage-taking unhelpful. "The actions that are taking place today, led by a small minority of individuals, are not helping as we work for a positive resolution of this situation," said Chris Schena, Caterpillar vice president with responsibility for manufacturing operations in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, in a statement. "The best way to resolve this matter is to continue the negotiations through the Works Council to find a solution that's fair to our employees and allows Caterpillar to remain a leader in a rapidly changing global marketplace," Schena said, adding that the company was "concerned for the safety of our employees." Benoit said all the workers wanted to do was negotiate with Caterpillar and they were upset that the company did not show up to two earlier scheduled negotiating sessions. The employees being held in their office were being allowed to get food, Benoit added. Police arrived at the scene two hours after the incident began but it had not been settled. Employees at a French 3M factory held a manager hostage for more than 24 hours Wednesday and Thursday of last week over a dispute about terms for laid-off staff. Luc Rousselet, who was unharmed, was allowed to leave the plant in Pithiviers, central France, early on Thursday morning after talks between unions and officials from 3M France. Earlier this month, the boss of Sony France was held overnight before workers freed him after he agreed to reopen talks on compensation when the factory closed. France has been hit by nationwide strikes twice in the past two months.

Caterpillar workers in France said management had failed to engage in talks about the proposed layoffs. The standoff marked at least the third occasion that month in which French employees facing workforce reductions had confined managers to their offices in an effort to force negotiations. In the two earlier cases, those detained were eventually freed without injury.

The latest confrontation began Tuesday morning at Caterpillar’s construction-equipment facility in Grenoble, in southeastern France. Union spokesman Nicolas Benoit said workers were upset because the company planned to eliminate more than 700 positions but refused to negotiate. He told CNN that the employees had no intention of hurting the executives.

One of the five people initially detained was allowed to leave Tuesday evening. Union representative Bernard Patrick identified him only as Mr. Petit, a human-resources director who had suffered a heart attack several weeks earlier and continued to have cardiac problems.

Patrick said the four people who remained inside were operations chief Nicolas Polutnik, two additional executives and Petit’s personal assistant. Roughly 500 other employees were demonstrating outside the building.

A senior Caterpillar official said the workers’ actions were making it harder to reach a solution.

Chris Schena, the Caterpillar vice president overseeing manufacturing in Europe, Africa and the Middle East, said in a statement that the conduct of a small minority that day was not contributing to efforts to achieve a constructive outcome.

Schena said the dispute should be addressed through continued discussions with the Works Council, with the aim of reaching an agreement that treated employees fairly while enabling Caterpillar to maintain its leading position in a quickly evolving global market. He added that the company was worried about its employees’ safety.

According to Benoit, the workers’ sole objective was to secure negotiations. Their frustration had increased after Caterpillar failed to attend two previously arranged bargaining meetings. He also said those being confined in the office were permitted to obtain food.

Police reached the location two hours after the incident started, but the dispute remained unresolved.

The episode followed a similar confrontation at a French 3M plant the previous week. Employees there detained manager Luc Rousselet for more than 24 hours on Wednesday and Thursday during a disagreement over conditions offered to laid-off workers. Rousselet, who was not harmed, was allowed to leave the factory in Pithiviers in central France early Thursday after unions held discussions with representatives of 3M France.

Earlier in the same month, Sony France’s chief was kept at a site overnight. Workers released him after he agreed to resume negotiations over compensation connected to the plant’s closure.

**French Caterpillar workers detain executives over planned layoffs**

**GRENOBLE, France —** Workers at a Caterpillar plant in southeastern France detained four company executives overnight in protest over plans to cut hundreds of jobs, union officials said.

The managers, including the head of Caterpillar’s French operations, were prevented from leaving company offices in Grenoble as employees demanded new negotiations over a restructuring plan affecting about 733 positions.

The executives were released unharmed after union representatives secured an agreement for further talks with management. Workers described the action as a last resort amid fears that the layoffs would devastate families and the local economy.

Caterpillar said the job cuts were necessary because the global economic downturn had sharply reduced demand for construction equipment. The U.S.-based manufacturer condemned the detention and called for negotiations to proceed without intimidation.

The incident was part of a wave of so-called “bossnappings” in France during the 2008-2009 financial crisis, when employees at several companies confined managers to workplaces to press for improved severance terms or changes to proposed layoffs.

French authorities monitored the situation but did not immediately intervene, reflecting the government’s cautious approach to escalating already tense labor disputes. No injuries were reported.

counterfactuals.output:
In late March 2009, workers at Caterpillar’s plants near Grenoble detained four senior managers during a dispute over plans to eliminate **733 jobs**, out of roughly 2,700 positions at the Grenoble and Échirolles sites.

Those confined included **Caterpillar France director Nicolas Polutnik**, the human-resources director, and two other executives. One manager was released early for health reasons; the others were freed unharmed after about a day when management agreed to resume negotiations with unions.

The episode was part of a broader French wave of recession-era labor militancy dubbed **“bossnapping.”** Employees at companies including Sony, 3M and Scapa had also confined managers, while workers at firms such as Continental staged occupations and confrontational protests over closures, layoffs and severance terms. Although technically illegal, such detentions generally ended peacefully and reflected mounting anger over job losses during the global financial crisis.

counterfactuals.prompt: What happened when hundreds of French workers protested Caterpillar’s plan to cut more than 700 jobs? Provide a detailed news article with statements from union and company representatives.
counterfactuals.output:
## French Caterpillar Workers Detain Managers in Protest Over 733 Planned Job Cuts

**GRENOBLE, France —** Hundreds of workers at Caterpillar’s operations in southeastern France staged an angry protest after the U.S. heavy-equipment manufacturer announced plans to eliminate more than 700 jobs, with some employees preventing four company executives from leaving a plant overnight.

The dispute erupted at Caterpillar facilities in Grenoble and nearby Échirolles, where the company planned to cut **733 positions** as demand for construction machinery collapsed during the global economic downturn.

During the protest, workers occupied administrative offices and barricaded the exits, keeping four senior managers inside. Among those detained was the head of Caterpillar’s French operations. The executives were not reported to have been injured and were allowed food and access to telephones, but employees refused to let them leave until management agreed to resume negotiations.

### Union says action was intended to force negotiations

Union representatives said workers had taken the action because Caterpillar had refused to offer adequate alternatives to compulsory redundancies or sufficiently improve severance terms.

CGT union representative **Nicolas Benoît** said the employees’ principal demand was the reopening of talks over the restructuring plan. Union officials emphasized that the managers had not been physically threatened and characterized the incident as pressure tactics rather than violence.

“We want negotiations to restart,” Benoît said in remarks reported at the time. He argued that Caterpillar had the financial resources to provide stronger guarantees and compensation for employees who stood to lose their jobs.

Workers also demanded that the company consider measures such as reduced working hours, transfers, early retirement and voluntary departures before imposing layoffs. Several hundred employees gathered outside the offices, chanting and supporting those occupying the building.

### Company condemns confinement but agrees to more talks

Caterpillar representatives described the confinement of the executives as unacceptable and said management wanted the dispute settled peacefully. The company maintained that the job reductions were necessary because the global recession had sharply reduced orders for earth-moving and construction equipment.

Management said Caterpillar had already been discussing a social plan with employee representatives and remained willing to negotiate, but insisted that executives should not be prevented from leaving their workplace.

After intervention by local officials and assurances that negotiations would resume, the four managers were released. They had been held for roughly a day.

Caterpillar later said it was relieved that the executives had been freed and reiterated that the company would continue talks with unions. It also stressed that the restructuring reflected a steep and sudden fall in demand rather than a decision directed specifically against French employees.

### Part of a wider wave of French labor unrest

The episode became one of the best-known examples of the so-called **“bossnapping”** protests that occurred in France during the financial crisis. Workers at several companies temporarily detained managers in an effort to obtain better redundancy packages or force employers back to the negotiating table.

Although such detentions were technically unlawful, they were generally brief and nonviolent. The Caterpillar incident highlighted the growing anger among French industrial workers, who argued that employees were being made to bear the cost of a crisis created elsewhere.

The release of the managers ended the immediate standoff, but it did not resolve the underlying dispute. Unions continued mobilizing against the proposed 733 job losses and pressed Caterpillar to reduce the number of compulsory departures and improve compensation for those affected.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the “bossnapping” of Caterpillar executives by workers in Grenoble, with context about similar incidents at 3M and Sony France and recent nationwide strikes.
counterfactuals.output:
### Caterpillar managers held by workers in Grenoble

**Grenoble, France — April 2009:** Workers at Caterpillar’s plants in Grenoble and nearby Échirolles detained four company executives overnight after negotiations over planned job cuts broke down. The U.S. construction-equipment manufacturer was seeking to eliminate roughly **733 jobs** from a local workforce of about 2,700.

Union members blocked the managers—including the head of Caterpillar France—from leaving an office. The executives were reportedly given food and were not physically harmed. They were released the following morning after management agreed to reopen negotiations over severance terms and measures to reduce compulsory redundancies.

The episode was quickly labeled a **“bossnapping,”** the French media’s term for workers temporarily confining managers to force negotiations. Police generally avoided intervening, in part because the managers were not reported to be in immediate danger.

### Similar incidents at 3M and Sony France

The Caterpillar action followed other high-profile confrontations:

- **Sony France:** In March 2009, employees at a plant in Pontonx-sur-l’Adour, southwestern France, barricaded the site and held Sony France president Serge Foucher and another executive overnight. The plant, employing about **300 people**, was due to close. The managers were released after agreeing to further talks over redundancy compensation.

- **3M:** Later that month, workers at 3M’s Pithiviers factory held a manager overnight during a dispute over approximately **110 planned job losses**. He was released after assurances that negotiations would continue.

In each case, unions portrayed the action as a last resort after conventional bargaining had failed. Employers and government officials condemned unlawful detention, although the incidents ended without reported violence.

### Wider climate of labor unrest

The “bossnappings” occurred amid deep anxiety over the global financial crisis and recession. France had recently seen two major nationwide days of strikes and demonstrations, on **January 29 and March 19, 2009**. Public- and private-sector workers protested layoffs, declining purchasing power, public-service reductions and President Nicolas Sarkozy’s economic policies.

Unions claimed that as many as several million people joined the March demonstrations, while police issued lower estimates. The actions reflected a broader conviction among many French workers that employees were being made to bear the cost of a crisis created by corporate and financial leaders.

Although detaining executives was not a normal union tactic and remained illegal, the Caterpillar, Sony and 3M incidents became symbols of the unusually confrontational mood in French industrial relations during the recession.
